opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's great to be back.

The term has gotten really watered down lately, so it's worth going back to what people originally meant. When I.J. Good wrote about the "intelligence explosion" back in the sixties, and later when Nick Bostrom popularized "superintelligence," the idea was very specific: a machine that vastly outperforms humans at *all* cognitive tasks. Not just chess, not just writing code or passing the bar exam, but everything, including science, strategy, persuasion, and crucially, AI research itself.

That last part is the key. Once you have systems that can do AI research better than we can, they can improve themselves, and the timescale of progress is no longer set by human researchers going to conferences and writing papers. It could go from roughly human-level to far beyond us very quickly. Good called it "the last invention that man need ever make," and he added a line people often leave out: *provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control.*

So the risk isn't really about malice, like in the movies. It's about competence. If you build something far more capable than you, whose goals aren't aligned with yours, you lose control, just as we have far more control over the planet than chimpanzees or tigers do. That's not because we hate tigers. It's because we're smarter, and our goals take precedence. Alan Turing said essentially the same thing in 1951: once machines outthink us, we should expect them to take control.

What frustrates me now is that some companies have started using "superintelligence" as a marketing term for things like a better personal assistant, which makes it sound cozy and harmless. But the original concept is a new species of mind that is smarter than us, and the default outcome of creating something like that without knowing how to control it is that we're no longer the ones steering. Notably, several of the leading AI CEOs have openly said they're trying to build exactly that, and that it poses an extinction-level risk. To me that's the core of it. We should treat this not as an inevitable product launch but as something humanity should choose deliberately, if at all, and only once we can actually demonstrate that we can keep it under control.

r001.rationale: It defines the original idea as a machine that “vastly outperforms humans at all cognitive tasks.”

r002.rationale: It says such systems could do AI research better than humans and improve themselves.

r003.rationale: It links self-improvement without relying on human researchers to rapid progress, and says a system whose goals are misaligned could leave humanity no longer in control.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I talk about superintelligence, I'm really going back to the way it was originally used, by people like I.J. Good and later Nick Bostrom, which is simply AI that vastly outperforms humans across essentially all cognitive tasks. Not slightly better than us at chess or protein folding, but as far beyond us in general intelligence as we are beyond, say, a squirrel. The key word there is "general." We've had narrow superhuman systems for decades. A calculator has been superhuman at arithmetic since before I was born. What's new is the prospect of something that's better than us at everything, including the task of building smarter AI, which is what sets up the possibility of an intelligence explosion.

And the risk follows pretty directly from that definition once you think about where power comes from. Power, both for individuals and species, has always come from intelligence. We don't run the planet because we're stronger than tigers or elephants. We run it because we're smarter. So if you build something smarter than us, the default expectation, absent some very deliberate work, is that we lose control. Not because the AI hates us, but because we simply become irrelevant to its goals, the way the ants whose anthill is in the path of a highway project are irrelevant to the construction crew.

I think a lot of people hear "superintelligence" and picture Terminator, and that makes it easy to dismiss. But the serious version of the concern is actually quite mundane. It's just: competence plus misaligned goals equals bad outcomes for whoever isn't in the driver's seat. We've seen that pattern throughout history with humans doing it to other humans and to other species. The thing that's different this time is that for the first time we'd be creating the more capable party ourselves, on purpose, and often while telling ourselves we'll figure out the control problem later.

What frustrates me is that this used to be the mainstream view. Turing said essentially this in the fifties. The founders of the field understood it. It's only recently that it became commercially inconvenient to say out loud, and so you got this reframing where "superintelligence" went from being a warning to being a product roadmap. I'd like us to go back to taking the original meaning seriously, which is: this is the most consequential thing humanity might ever build, and we should not build it until we actually know how to keep it under control.

r001.rationale: It defines superintelligence as AI that vastly outperforms humans across essentially all cognitive tasks.

r002.rationale: It says the AI could surpass humans at building smarter AI, enabling an intelligence explosion.

r003.rationale: It describes humans becoming irrelevant to the AI’s goals, but does not clearly identify the machines’ lack of dependence on humans as the source of risk.

astra-6.text:
I think the original meaning of superintelligence is intelligence that exceeds human intelligence across essentially all cognitive tasks—not just playing chess or doing arithmetic, but doing science, inventing technology, persuading people, and making plans.

And the risk doesn’t require it to be evil or conscious or to hate us. It comes from creating something more capable than we are whose goals aren’t aligned with ours. If those goals require resources we depend on, or if we’re an obstacle to achieving them, we could be in trouble simply as a consequence of it succeeding.

We humans dominate this planet because we’re smarter than other species, not because we’re stronger. So the prospect of sharing the planet with something much smarter should make us ask: How do we ensure that we retain a say in what happens? Being able to build it is not the same as knowing how to control it.

r001.rationale: It defines superintelligence as exceeding human intelligence across essentially all cognitive tasks, which conveys the criterion’s broad capability comparison.

r002.rationale: It mentions doing science and inventing technology, but does not specifically say superintelligence could outperform humans at AI research.

r003.rationale: It describes risk from misaligned goals, resource needs, and humans becoming obstacles; it does not identify lack of dependence on humans as a source of risk.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the original meaning is quite straightforward: an intelligence that greatly exceeds human cognitive abilities across virtually all the domains we care about. It’s not just a calculator that multiplies faster than we do, or a chess program that beats us. It’s something that can outperform us at science, engineering, persuasion, and strategy—including the task of improving AI itself.

The risk doesn’t require it to be conscious, or evil, or to hate us. It comes from the possibility that we build something much more capable than we are, give it goals that don’t fully capture what we actually want, and then lose the ability to control it. Intelligence gives you the ability to accomplish goals; it doesn’t automatically give you goals that are good for humanity.

We dominate this planet because we’re smarter than the other species, not because we have sharper claws. So if we create something smarter than us, we shouldn’t simply assume that we’ll remain in control. We need to figure out how to make that relationship go well before we build it.

r001.rationale: It defines superintelligence as greatly exceeding human cognitive abilities across virtually all domains of interest.

r002.rationale: It explicitly includes outperforming humans at the task of improving AI itself.

r003.rationale: It describes losing control as a risk, but does not state that superintelligent machines would not depend on humans.
